title: Manhood: A Bible Study on What a Man Is For
subtitle: A five-session study on masculinity, strength, and the man Jesus was.
summary:
This study is for men who are tired of being handed two versions of manhood and told to pick one. There's the swaggering one that mistakes volume for strength, and the soft one that mistakes absence for peace, and most men suspect the truth is neither. Over five sessions we'll ask what manhood is actually for once the culture-war cartoons are cleared away. We'll look at the father wound and the God who calls himself "Father of the fatherless" (Psalm 68:5). We'll look at strength under control in the man who wept, washed feet and drove the money changers out of the temple. We'll look at friendship and the silence that is quietly killing men who won't say they're drowning. And we'll end with servant leadership, set against domination, and the calling every man has to raise or mentor the next one.

It's built so a busy man or a volunteer can lead it without long preparation. Every question carries a note on what's behind it, and every session ends in prayer rather than in the performance men so often bring into a room of other men.

This study doesn't stand over men and grade them. Many of us have been the man who confused controlling a room with leading it, who went silent for days rather than admit he was afraid, who reached for anger because it felt more like strength than the truth did. I'm in that number. The study refuses both counterfeits with the same firmness. It won't baptize the domineering man who reads Scripture as a permit for his temper, and it won't excuse the passive man who calls his absence humility. It holds up one man as the measure, the one who had all the strength there is and bent it entirely toward the good of the people in front of him.
audience: Men, fathers, sons, and the small groups and mentoring pairs that carry them

sessions.title: What Manhood Is For, Past the Caricatures
sessions.aim: To clear away the two culture-war caricatures of masculinity, the domineering strongman and the passive nice guy, and to recover manhood as something God gives for a purpose rather than something proven against other men, refusing both the swagger that mistakes volume for strength and the softness that mistakes absence for peace.
sessions.summary:
Plenty of young men will tell you they don't know how to be a man, because everyone who has tried to tell them was selling something. One voice says a real man dominates, wins, never backs down and takes what he wants. The other says the whole idea is toxic and he ought to apologize for having shoulders. He's standing between two cartoons, and neither one will make him a man.

So the question of this session isn't which side of the culture war to join. It's what manhood is for. Scripture doesn't begin with conquest. It begins with a garden and a man put in it "to work it and keep it" (Genesis 2:15). There's a strong case, made by many books and voices, that the church has produced too many merely harmless men, and it's right that the passive man is a real failure. The first failure of manhood in the Bible isn't Cain's violence but Adam's silence. But that call to strength keeps sliding into the caricature it meant to correct, until strength means getting your way.

Both counterfeits run on the same fear. Real manhood is strength given a purpose outside itself: the man who works and keeps, who takes up responsibility no one assigned him, who is strong the way a roof is strong, for the sake of what it shelters.

keyScripture.why: "Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love" (1 Corinthians 16:13-14). Paul puts the call to strength and the call to love in the same breath, so neither the strongman nor the nice guy can claim the verse.

discussion.q: Most of us picked up a picture of manhood from somewhere: the strongman who dominates, or the nice guy who apologizes for existing. Which picture did you absorb, and where did you get it?
discussion.behind: Start by bringing out the script each man is running before you define anything. Most men have swallowed one picture and are quietly ashamed they can't pull it off, or rejected one so hard they backed into the other. Don't settle it yet. Just get the inherited picture said out loud, and notice how often it came from a screen, a locker room, or a father, present or absent.

discussion.q: Read Genesis 2:15. God puts the man in the garden "to work it and keep it" before Scripture says a word about strength or authority. What changes when manhood starts with a responsibility given rather than a rank won?
discussion.behind: The culture tends to measure a man by what he conquers or consumes. Genesis measures him by what he's charged to cultivate and protect. Help the room feel both the relief and the weight of that: manhood is a stewardship handed to you, not a place you have to fight your way into against other men.

discussion.q: Read Genesis 3:6. The woman gives the fruit "to her husband who was with her." What do you make of the fact that he was right there and said nothing? Where have you called your own passivity peace, or humility, or picking your battles?
discussion.behind: Give the call to recover masculine strength its due, then turn it inward. Adam's failure was silence and absence while present. Press gently on where each man goes quiet and calls it wisdom, avoids and calls it patience, disappears and calls it not wanting conflict. Go first and name your own retreat.

discussion.q: The same voices that rightly name the passive man often slide toward the strongman, until strength just means getting your way. Where have you confused being strong with being loud, being right, or never being crossed?
discussion.behind: Now turn the question the other way so the room can't simply pick the strongman as the cure. Counterfeit strength is fragile. It's threatened by any challenge and needs the last word. Help men see that the man who can't be contradicted isn't strong but scared, and that the fear of looking weak is running the whole performance.

discussion.q: Paul says "act like men, be strong" and then "Let all that you do be done in love" (1 Corinthians 16:13-14). If your strength is for something outside yourself, who is it for right now, and would they say they feel sheltered by it?
discussion.behind: Land the session on purpose, not on the culture war. Push each man past the abstract to the actual people under his roof, literal and otherwise. The test of a man's strength isn't how much he has but what it's bent toward. Ask gently whether the people nearest him experience his strength as shelter or as weather they have to survive.

objections.objection: This whole conversation about masculinity is the problem. There is no such thing as biblical manhood, only human virtue, and telling men to be men just smuggles in a bunch of cultural stereotypes and dresses them up as Scripture.
objections.response: A great deal of this is right. Much of what gets sold as biblical manhood is a mid-century cultural picture with a verse stapled to it: the pickup truck, the grill, and the refusal to cry treated as holiness. That's worth rejecting, and the study rejects it. But notice the overcorrection. Scripture does speak to men as men. It tells them to "act like men, be strong" in the same sentence it tells them to do everything in love (1 Corinthians 16:13-14), and it holds up particular men and particular failures as men's failures: Adam's silence, David's abuse of power. To flatten all of that into generic virtue is to lose something the text won't let us lose, that God made humanity "male and female" (Genesis 1:27) on purpose and calls each to a particular faithfulness. The answer to a bad picture of manhood is a true one, not none at all. Men who are told manhood means nothing don't become free. They drift, and someone worse is always waiting to hand them a counterfeit.

objections.objection: Real men lead, provide, and protect, and the reason the culture is falling apart is that men have gone soft. The church needs to stop apologizing and call men back to being strong, decisive, and in charge.
objections.response: Half of this is true, and the half that's false is dangerous. Passivity is a real failure, the first one in Scripture, and the Bible really does call men to strength and courage. But watch "leading, providing and protecting" slide into "being in charge," because that's where the strongman hides. The man Scripture holds up as the measure did lead and provide and protect, and he did it by washing feet, by weeping, by laying his life down, by spending his strength entirely on the people in front of him and never once on himself. Strength isn't the problem, and softness isn't the cure. The question is what the strength is for. A man who is strong for himself isn't a leader. He's a hazard. The culture isn't suffering for lack of men in charge so much as from men who confused being in charge with being good.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Are you more tempted to prove you're a man by dominating a room, or to dodge the risk of manhood by disappearing from it? And what are you afraid of underneath both?
sessions.practice: This week, catch yourself once in your usual counterfeit. If you lean toward the strongman, notice the moment you need the last word or the room's agreement, and let it go on purpose without collapsing. If you lean toward the passive man, notice the moment you go quiet to avoid conflict, and say the true thing, kindly and out loud. Don't announce either one as growth. Just do the harder thing, and write down what you were actually afraid of when you did it.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you made us men on purpose, and you put the first man in a garden to work it and keep it before you said a word about who was in charge. Forgive us the caricatures we swallowed, the strongman who is only a scared boy shouting and the passive man who calls his absence peace. We've used volume to hide fear, and silence to hide the same fear. Teach us the strength that is a roof and not a storm, the courage that steps forward and the humility that doesn't need to win. Make us men whose strength the people around us can rest under. And where we never had a man to show us, be the Father who does. Amen.
reflection: Which picture of manhood did I inherit, and how much of what I do is still a performance of it?
Where have I called my passivity humility, or my domination leadership, so I wouldn't have to see either for what it is?
What is my strength actually for, and would the people closest to me say they feel sheltered by it or braced against it?
sessions.teaching:
Think of a young man who'll tell you, more plainly than most men manage, that he doesn't know how to be a man, because everyone who has tried to tell him was selling something. One set of voices says a real man dominates, wins, never backs down, takes what he wants and calls the taking strength. Another set says the whole idea of manhood is toxic and he should more or less apologize for having shoulders. He's standing in the middle of the culture war over masculinity, being handed two cartoons, and it hasn't occurred to anyone that neither one is going to make him a man. So the question I want to start with isn't which side of that war to join. It's what manhood is actually for, because you can't grow into something you've only ever seen drawn as a caricature.

Notice where Scripture starts, because it isn't where either side starts. It doesn't open with the warrior or the king or the man who takes. It opens with a garden. "The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it" (Genesis 2:15). Before any culture had written him a line of script, the man was given labor and responsibility. The first thing said over him isn't "dominate." It's closer to "cultivate and protect."

There's a strong case for recovering masculine strength, and it deserves to be heard first, because it's making a real point against a real failure. A whole shelf of books and a chorus of voices have said that men were made for weight and risk and burden, that the church has too often turned out men who are merely harmless, domesticated and safe, and that a man with no strength to offer isn't gentle, he's absent. The softer voices need to hear that, because the first failure of manhood in the Bible isn't Cain's violence. It's Adam's silence. While the serpent works on the woman, Genesis says she "gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate" (Genesis 3:6). He was right there. He said nothing, did nothing, protected nothing, and then he ate. The first failure of the first man was passivity, a man who was present and might as well not have been.

So that call to strength isn't wrong about the passive man. But watch what keeps happening to it, because it slides, almost every time, into the very caricature it set out to correct. The call to strength turns into a permit for temper. The call to leadership turns into a demand to be in charge. The call to courage turns into the man who can never be crossed, who reads every disagreement as disrespect and mistakes getting his way for godliness.

Most of us know both counterfeits from the inside. A boy with no man to learn from builds his picture of manhood out of whatever looks like strength, and for a lot of men what looks most like strength is control: the managed room, the won argument, the anger that feels more like power than the truth ever does. And many of us have gone the other way too, gone quiet and called it keeping the peace, when it was really Adam in the garden again, present and useless, letting something go wrong because speaking up felt like too much risk. Plenty of us have done both.

Here's what cuts against both sides at once. The loud counterfeit and the quiet counterfeit are the same thing underneath, because both run on fear. The strongman is terrified of looking weak, so he shouts. The passive man is terrified of what manhood might cost him, so he vanishes. Neither one is strong. And the answer isn't a blend of the two, a little dominance softened with a little niceness. It's something else entirely: strength given a purpose outside itself.

The man in the garden is strong the way a roof is strong. Nobody builds a roof so people can admire it. They build it so that what's underneath stays dry. His strength isn't for winning and it isn't for hiding. It's for working and keeping, for tending what's been entrusted to him and protecting it at cost. Paul puts it in a sentence neither caricature can survive: "Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love" (1 Corinthians 16:13-14). Strength and love are commanded in the same breath. Any manhood that keeps only one of them has already become a lie.

scriptureStudy.note: "The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it." Manhood begins in stewardship, in labor and protection given before any culture assigns a role. A man is defined first by what he's charged to tend and guard, not by what he conquers.
"She also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate." The first failure of manhood in Scripture isn't aggression but passivity. Adam is there, present and silent, protecting nothing.

"Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong." Paul really does call men to strength and courage, so those who want to recover masculine strength aren't wrong to hear it. What matters is the next verse, which won't let strength stand alone.

"Let all that you do be done in love." The strength of verse 13 is bent toward love in the same breath, so no man can quote the call to be strong without also being handed the purpose the strength exists for. Strength without this verse turns into menace.

"And what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?" The measure of a man here isn't dominance but justice done, kindness loved and humility walked, three things the strongman can't fake and the passive man can't avoid.

"He is like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season." The picture of a rooted life isn't the conqueror but the tree, strong because it's planted, fruitful because it's fed, and useful to everything in its shade.

"Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness." Paul's charge to the younger man he's training puts gentleness on the list of things to chase, the very quality the strongman despises. Gentleness here is strength under command, not weakness.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, look at the history behind the confusion men feel now, because it isn't timeless. For much of human history many boys learned manhood at a father's side, working alongside him in the field or the forge or the shop, so that becoming a man was a slow handing-down watched up close. Nancy Pearcey, in The Toxic War on Masculinity (2023), traces how the Industrial Revolution moved much of that work out of the home and sent fathers away to the factory and the office, breaking the daily apprenticeship and leaving boys to assemble manhood from their peers, and later from screens. That helps explain why manhood came to be performed rather than received, proven against other boys rather than handed down by a father.

Set beside it the secular men's movement that Robert Bly gave voice to in Iron John (1990). It grieved the father wound and the loss of male initiation and reached back to myth to fill the hole. It named the ache well, even where its answer went astray. Then take the theological turn. Charles Taylor described the modern "buffered self," sealed off and self-defining. A manhood with no father to receive it from and no purpose outside itself becomes exactly that: a self that has to make its own meaning by performance. That's why the strongman has to keep proving and the passive man has to keep hiding. Both are a man trying to become a man alone. The hunger for strong men is good and God-given. Ask where the broken handing-down of manhood has shaped your own picture of it without your consent.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group is respected, capable, and quietly proud that he isn't like the angry, domineering men he grew up around. He's gentle and agreeable and slow to make waves, and he hears the material on the strongman with obvious relief, sure it isn't about him.

Honor him before you press. He's right that he has avoided a real sin, and his refusal to dominate is a real grace worth naming. But notice how quickly he put the whole danger in the other caricature. The session had a second half, the passive man who calls his absence peace. His gentleness may be the fruit of the Spirit. It may also be, in places, an old fear of conflict wearing a nicer name.

Don't let him file the whole session as a critique of men who aren't in the room. You might ask, gently, where his agreeableness has become a way of not risking anything, and whether the people who depend on him have ever needed him to be strong and found him quietly gone.

sessions.title: The Father Wound and the God Who Fathers the Fatherless
sessions.aim: To name the father wound plainly, the mark left by a father who was absent, or present and cold, or present and cruel, and to bring it to the God who calls himself "Father of the fatherless," refusing both the bitterness that lives in the wound and the denial that pretends it left no mark, and pointing to the healing that comes from being fathered by God rather than from finally getting from an earthly father what he never gave.
sessions.summary:
The wound a missing or failing father leaves doesn't announce itself. It hides, and decades later it surfaces as a hunger for approval no achievement satisfies, an anger that surprises you, or a quiet certainty that you're on your own and always were. Many men were wounded by their fathers in one of three ways: the father who left, the father who was there but cold, and the father who was there and cruel. So the question isn't whether a man carries a wound. It's what he does with it.

There's a strong case for simply moving on. A man shouldn't blame his father for his life, and dwelling on it can turn into self-pity. That's partly true; bitterness is a real trap. But a wound you refuse to name doesn't heal. It goes underground and steers from there, and the man most controlled by his father is often the one who insists his father doesn't matter.

God doesn't answer the father wound with a technique. He offers himself. "Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation" (Psalm 68:5). The healing isn't finally getting from your earthly father what he never gave, because most men never will. It's being fathered by God now, receiving as a gift the approval you were starving for, so you can stop demanding it from a man who can't give it, living or dead.

keyScripture.why: "Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation" (Psalm 68:5). God names himself by the very role a missing or failing father left empty. He isn't a distant deity but a Father who takes the vacant place and defends the ones no one else defended.

discussion.q: Without performing and without blaming, what was your father to you? Was he gone, there but distant, there and hard, or something else, and what did that leave in you?
discussion.behind: This opens the tenderest door in the study, so open it carefully. Men will want to defend their fathers or wave the question off. Give permission to tell the truth without disloyalty, to say a father was loved and still left a mark. Some men had good fathers; let them say so. Don't rush anyone. The goal isn't to put fathers on trial but to name what was there and what was missing.

discussion.q: A father wound often shows up years later as a hunger for approval, an anger out of proportion to the moment, or a certainty that you're on your own. Where do you see something old steering your adult life?
discussion.behind: Move from the past to the present, because the point isn't the history but its grip now. Help men connect the buried thing to the visible pattern: the workaholism chasing an approval that never comes, the anger too big for the moment, the refusal to depend on anyone. Go first and name yours.

discussion.q: Many of us were taught that a real man just gets over it and doesn't blame his father for his life. What's true in that, and where does refusing to look at the wound keep it in control of you?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. Bitterness and blame are real traps, and endless grievance isn't healing. But refusing to look at a wound isn't strength; it's avoidance. Help the room see the difference between naming a wound so it can heal and nursing one to excuse yourself.

discussion.q: Read Psalm 68:5 and Psalm 27:10. God calls himself "Father of the fatherless," and the psalmist says, "For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in." What's your gut reaction to being fathered by God, and what makes it hard to receive?
discussion.behind: This is the center of the session, and it's hard for men to receive, not just to understand. For some, the word Father is damaged. Handle that with care. The point isn't that God is a better version of your dad, but that he's a Father whose approval you never have to earn and can't lose. Let men sit with why that's so hard to believe about themselves.

discussion.q: At Jesus' baptism the Father says, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17), before Jesus has done a single miracle. Whose approval are you still waiting on, and what would it free you to do if you stopped waiting?
discussion.behind: Close on the freedom here. Many men organize their whole lives around a word from a father who is unable or unwilling or no longer alive to say it. Name that gently. In Christ the approval comes before the work, as a gift. Let the room feel the release, not as closure with an earthly father but as being fathered by God.

objections.objection: All this father wound talk is just an excuse. Plenty of men had bad fathers and turned out fine, and blaming your dad for who you are now is weak and self-pitying. At some point you are a grown man responsible for yourself.
objections.response: This objection is guarding something true, and it's worth guarding: responsibility. A man is accountable for what he does with his life. No father's failure excuses cruelty or cowardice, and a grievance nursed into an identity is its own kind of chain. The fear of self-pity isn't foolish. But naming a wound isn't the same as blaming it. You can take full responsibility for your life and still tell the truth about what shaped it. In fact you can't take responsibility for a wound you won't look at, because the unnamed wound runs things from underground, out of sight and out of reach. Refusing to look at it isn't strength. It's handing your father the steering wheel and insisting you're driving. Responsibility begins with the truth, and the strongest thing a man can do with a father wound is name it in the light and bring it to God.

objections.objection: If God is a father, that does not help me, it makes it worse, because my father is exactly why I want nothing to do with the word. Telling me God is a Father just puts the face of the man who hurt me on the God I am supposed to trust.
objections.response: Take this with complete seriousness. For a man whose father was absent or cold or cruel, the word Father isn't neutral; it's a wound, and anyone who says "God is a father" as if that settles everything hasn't sat with that pain. So hear it carefully. Scripture doesn't say God is like your father, only bigger. It points to a Father your father was meant to reflect and failed to, sometimes so badly that he hid the original entirely. When Jesus shows us the Father, he tells of a father who sees his wasteful son "while he was still a long way off," and "felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him" (Luke 15:20). The point isn't to project your father onto God. It's that God offers to heal the very word your father damaged, to be the Father who doesn't leave, doesn't go cold and doesn't turn cruel, so that over time the name that was a wound can become the place you're safe. That may take a long time, and it's all right if it does.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Whose approval are you still, at your age, quietly organizing your life to win? What would change if you believed you already had a Father who was pleased with you?
sessions.practice: This week, do two things privately. First, tell God plainly about your father, out loud if you can, without performing and without blaming, just saying what was there and what was missing. Second, when you catch yourself chasing the old approval, at work, in a room, in the mirror, stop and remind yourself that you already have a Father, and that in Christ his word over you is settled and can't be earned or lost. Write down what rises in you the first time you try to believe it.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father of the fatherless, you know exactly what was and wasn't at the head of each of our tables: the chair that was empty, the man who was there but far away, the one who was there and dangerous. Some of us have carried that for decades and called it nothing, and it has steered us the whole time, chasing an approval that never came, braced for a blow, sure we were on our own. You aren't a bigger version of the man who failed us. You are the Father he was meant to show us and couldn't. Take the empty chair. Say over us the word we spent our lives trying to earn. And let us, fathered by grace, become men who father, so that the wound stops with us. Amen.
reflection: What exactly did my father leave in me, through absence, coldness or cruelty, or through a goodness I've never thanked God for? Have I ever named it plainly instead of defending or dismissing it?
Where is the old wound still steering, in my hunger for approval, my surprising anger, or my refusal to depend on anyone?
Do I actually believe God offers to be my Father now, and what in me resists an approval I didn't earn and can't lose?
sessions.teaching:
The wound a missing father leaves doesn't announce itself. It doesn't walk up and introduce itself as a father wound. It hides. A man can go thirty years insisting he's fine, that his father didn't matter, that he never thinks about it, and be telling the truth as far as he can see, while the wound steers his life from somewhere he can't see.

It surfaces later, in disguise. It comes as a hunger for approval that no achievement satisfies: the promotion that should have been enough and wasn't, the applause that emptied out by morning. It comes as an anger that surprises you, far bigger than the small thing that set it off, because the small thing brushed against the old thing. And it comes as a deep certainty that you're on your own, that no one is coming, that you'd better handle it yourself because that's how it's always been.

So I don't want to ask whether you were wounded by your father, because a great many men were, in one of three ways. There's the father who left, by divorce or death or the door: the empty chair. There's the father who was there in body and absent in every other way, at the table and a thousand miles away behind his eyes. And there's the father who was there and cruel, whose attention was worse than his absence would have been. Some men were well fathered, and that's a gift to thank God for. But most men are somewhere in those three, and the real question is what a man does with it.

The strong case for just getting over it deserves a fair hearing, because it sounds like strength and it's what most men were taught. A real man, the argument goes, doesn't blame his father for his life. Dwelling on it is self-pity, and the manly thing is to shrug it off, take responsibility and move on. There's something true in that, and I want to grant it fully. Bitterness is a real trap, and blame can grow into a whole identity, a man who explains every failure by pointing back at his dad and never grows up. That man isn't free either.

But there's a lie folded into the manly refusal. The wound you won't name doesn't heal. It doesn't go away when you stop looking at it. It goes underground and runs things from there, and the man most completely controlled by his father is very often the one who insists, with real conviction, that his father doesn't matter to him at all. A man can tell himself for years that growing up without a father made him strong and self-reliant, a plain fact about his past and nothing more, while the whole time it shapes how he leads, how he loves, how badly he needs respect, and how hard it is for him to depend on anyone or believe anyone will stay.

Here's the strangest and best thing in this session. God doesn't respond to the father wound with a technique. He doesn't hand men a five-step process for closure. He does something far more personal. He offers himself as a Father. "Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation" (Psalm 68:5). Read it slowly. It doesn't say God will help you make peace with your absent father from a comfortable distance. It says God takes up that role himself. A psalmist who knew abandonment wrote, "For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in" (Psalm 27:10). God becomes, to the abandoned, the very thing they were abandoned by.

That's where the healing is, if a man can receive it. The healing isn't getting from your earthly father, at long last, what he never gave you, because the hard truth is that most men never will. The father who couldn't say it at thirty won't say it at seventy, many of those fathers have died, and the reconciliation you've been waiting for may not come in the form you wanted. If your healing depends on that, you'll wait your whole life. But the gospel offers something better than the closure you can't get. It offers to father you now. At Jesus' baptism, before a single miracle or sermon, the Father said, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17). In Christ, God speaks to his adopted children with the same love, the approval given before the work, not as a wage you finally earn. When a man begins, even slowly, to believe that, something loosens. He can stop demanding from a man, living or dead, what that man was never able to give, because he's being fathered at last by the One who can.

scriptureStudy.note: "Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation." God names himself by the very role a missing father left empty. He isn't distant; he takes the vacant place and defends the ones no one else defended.

"For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in." Scripture names abandonment without softening it and then answers it, not with a technique for closure but with a God who takes in the one the parents put out.

"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him." Jesus shows the Father as one who runs to the son who wasted everything, the opposite of the cold or cruel father, moved with compassion at the first sight of a son coming home.

Paul says believers "have received the Spirit of adoption as sons," by whom they cry out to God as "Abba," Father. Fatherlessness is answered by adoption, a sonship that is permanent, and by a Spirit who teaches the fatherless to use the most intimate name for God, the very word the father wound made hardest to say.

"See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God." John marvels at a love that makes us God's children, an identity given rather than earned, which is exactly the approval the wounded man keeps trying to work for.

"And I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty." God makes the offer directly, in the first person, as a covenant commitment, not a comforting image.

"This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased." The Father says this over Jesus before the ministry begins. In Christ, the adopted son hears love spoken before the work, the opposite of the wage the wounded man keeps trying to earn.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, take up the research on fatherlessness, and test it against Scripture rather than swallowing it whole or dismissing it for where it comes from. A large body of social research finds that children raised without an involved father face higher risks across a range of outcomes, and Warren Farrell and John Gray, in The Boy Crisis (2018), gather much of that work to argue that father absence is one of the most under-discussed causes of boys' struggles. Grant the finding its weight. It confirms in numbers what Scripture assumes in its stories: a father matters enormously, and his absence leaves a real mark. But notice what the data can and can't do. It can name the cost with real precision. It can't supply the cure, because no statistic can father a fatherless man.

Set it beside the secular men's work of Robert Bly and others, which grieved the father wound sincerely and reached for myth and ritual to fill it, naming the ache while missing where the healing comes from. Then take the theological turn. If the deepest father wound is healed not by finding the earthly father but by being fathered by God, then adoption isn't a dry legal footnote. For a wounded man it may be the most personally urgent truth in the New Testament: the fatherless are made sons, permanently, by grace. Sit with the difference between closure, which the world offers and often can't deliver, and adoption, which God offers and has already given in Christ. Handle all of it with care, because in almost any group of men there's one whose wound is fresh or severe, and the aim is never to rush a man past his grief into a slogan.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group speaks warmly about his father, says they had a great relationship, and grows visibly impatient with the whole idea of a father wound, calling it a therapy fad that lets weak men off the hook.

He isn't lying, and he may well have had a good father. Some men truly were well fathered, and the study should be glad for it and never manufacture a wound where there isn't one. But the heat of his impatience is worth a gentle question, because a man who was securely fathered rarely needs to attack the idea that others weren't. His reaction may be guarding a real gift. It may also be guarding a loyalty that won't let him say a true and hard thing about a father he loves.

Don't pry, and don't insist he's wounded when he may not be. Honor the good father if there was one. You might simply ask, later and privately, whether his certainty feels like peace or like armor, and let him know the room is safe if he ever wants to set the armor down.

memoryVerse.text: Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation.

sessions.title: Strength Under Control, the Man Jesus Was
sessions.aim: To hold up Jesus as the true measure of manhood, the man who wept openly, knelt to wash feet and drove the money changers out of the temple, and to define strength not as the absence of feeling or the presence of force but as power held under command, refusing both the picture that makes Jesus soft and the picture that makes the whip a permit for a man's temper.
sessions.summary:
Men can't agree on what strength is partly because we argue about it in the abstract and skip the concrete case in front of us: Jesus, who fits neither side's cartoon. Those who want a soft, harmless Jesus have to explain the whip and the overturned tables. Those who want a warrior Jesus who never showed weakness have to explain the tears, the basin and the towel.

Jesus answers the question of strength with a life. He wept at a friend's grave, and no one who watched thought him weak. He knelt and washed his disciples' feet, taking a servant's job, and it was the strongest thing in the room. He made "a whip of cords" (John 2:15) and cleared the temple, and that wasn't a loss of control. There's a real point in the men who love the whip and quote it against a church they find too soft: Jesus wasn't harmless. But the whip exposes the strongman, because Jesus was angry at wrong done to others and to his Father's house, and never once at an insult to himself.

Strength isn't the absence of feeling, or Jesus was weak when he wept. It isn't the presence of force, or he was strong only with the whip. It's power under control, all of it available and all of it aimed at the good of others rather than the defense of self. The man who could have appealed for "more than twelve legions of angels" (Matthew 26:53) let himself be led to the cross.

keyScripture.why: "Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city" (Proverbs 16:32). Scripture ranks the man who governs himself above the conqueror. Self-command, not force, is the higher strength, and it's the strength Jesus lived.

discussion.q: People who want a soft Jesus have to explain the whip, and people who want a warrior Jesus have to explain the tears. Which of the two is harder for you to fit into your picture of a strong man, and why?
discussion.behind: Start by bringing out each man's default Jesus. Most of us have quietly edited him down to the half that confirms our picture of strength. Help the room notice which half they skip, the weeping or the whip, because the half you can't explain is usually the half your idea of manhood most needs. Don't settle it yet.

discussion.q: Read John 11:32-36. "Jesus wept" (John 11:35), in front of a crowd, and no one there thought him weak. Where did you learn that a strong man doesn't show what he feels, and what has that lesson cost you?
discussion.behind: Many men were trained early that feeling is weakness and composure is strength, and the training runs deep. Help men connect the lesson to its cost: the numbness, the isolation, the sons watching a father who never lets them see anything. Jesus wept in public and lost no strength doing it. Go first if the room is guarded.

discussion.q: Read John 13:3-15. Jesus knows "that the Father had given all things into his hands" (John 13:3), and then he takes a towel and washes feet. Why is it so hard for men to believe that low service is strength rather than a loss of standing?
discussion.behind: Men are trained to protect their standing, and choosing to go low feels like losing rank. Notice what John says comes first: Jesus knew who he was and where he was going. Only the secure man can kneel. The fear of looking low is a tell. Ask where each man refuses the low service that would actually serve.

discussion.q: Read John 2:13-17. Jesus wasn't harmless, and the men who quote this scene against a soft church have a point. What's true in it, and where does the whip get used to justify a man's temper?
discussion.behind: This is where the session can go wrong, so hold both halves carefully. Holy anger is real, and a manhood with no capacity for it isn't more Christlike. But the whip was aimed at wrong done in God's house, never at an insult to Jesus himself, and that difference is everything. Help the room test their own anger by it, since the strongman's anger is almost always about himself.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 26:51-53. With every power at hand, Jesus tells Peter to put away his sword. Where in your life is your strength aimed at defending yourself rather than serving others, and what would it look like to aim it the way Jesus did?
discussion.behind: The whole session comes to rest on this definition: strength is power under command, aimed at the good of others rather than the defense of self. Push each man to find where his strength currently serves his reputation, his comfort or his need to be right, and to imagine it aimed differently. End on the cross as the measure, power fully held and fully given.

objections.objection: You are just giving me the soft Jesus, the gentle, feelings-first Jesus that the church already overuses. Men need a Jesus with a spine, and turning strength into washing feet and crying is exactly why the church has no men left in it.
objections.response: This objection has cut Jesus in half and kept the wrong lesson from the half it likes. The Jesus in this session isn't the soft one. He's the whole one, the same man who wept at the grave and made a whip and cleared the temple, and a picture that keeps only the whip is as edited as one that keeps only the tears. So grant the real point. Jesus had a spine. He wasn't harmless, and a limp, feelings-only Christ is a distortion the church does overuse. But look at what the whip was for: wrong done in God's house, not his own honor. When he was mocked and beaten and spat on, he didn't swing it. Before Pilate, "Jesus made no further answer" (Mark 15:5). That isn't a man with no spine. It's a man with total power under total control, a far rarer strength than the man who can't take an insult. The trouble isn't that the church made Jesus too gentle. It's that angry men keep quoting the whip and skipping the silence before Pilate.

objections.objection: So a real man is supposed to be emotional and cry and serve everyone. That just sounds like being a pushover with extra steps, and pushovers get walked on and cannot protect anyone.
objections.response: The fear here points at something real. A man who is only soft, who can't stand firm or protect anyone or say the hard true thing, isn't Christlike either, and the study has already named the passive man as a failure. But this confuses being under control with being controllable, and they're opposites. Jesus wept, and no one walked over him. He washed feet, and then he faced the powers of his day and went to the cross on purpose. "No one takes it from me," he said of his life, "but I lay it down of my own accord" (John 10:18). His strength answered to his Father and never to his own ego. A pushover is run by his fear of conflict. Jesus was run by his Father's will, which is why he could be gentle without being weak and fierce without being cruel. The goal isn't to make you soft. It's to put your strength under the one command that makes it safe, so you protect what should be protected and never wound to defend yourself.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When your strength comes out as anger, is it ever like the whip in the temple, aimed at real wrong done to others? Or is it almost always about an insult to you?
sessions.practice: This week, run your strength through the test Jesus sets. When anger rises, stop and ask one question: is this about a wrong done to someone else, or an insult to me? Let the answer decide what you do next. And find one place to take up the towel, one low, unseen service you'd normally consider beneath you, and do it on purpose. Write down what it showed you, whether an anger that turned out to be about your pride, or a fear that made kneeling feel like losing.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, you are the man we keep editing, because the whole of you won't fit the cartoons we prefer. You wept at a grave and lost no strength. You knelt with a basin and were the strongest one in the room. You made a whip for the wrong done in your Father's house and stayed silent when they struck your own face. Forgive us the strength we aim at our own defense, the anger that is only ever about us, the composure we mistake for courage, the standing we're too afraid to lay down. Teach us power under your command, all of it held and all of it given for others, the way you held yours all the way to the cross you could have refused. Make us strong the way you are strong. Amen.
reflection: Which half of Jesus do I edit out, the one who wept or the one who made the whip, and what does that tell me about my own idea of strength?
Where is my anger really about an insult to me rather than a wrong done to someone else, and what would it take to tell the difference in the moment?
Is my strength under control, answering to God, or is it controllable, run by my fear of conflict or my need to defend myself?
sessions.teaching:
Men can't agree on what strength is partly because we keep arguing about it in theory and never look long enough at the one man who had all of it. We trade slogans and caricatures and walk right past the concrete case standing in front of us: Jesus, fully a man, who refuses to fit either side's cartoon.

Think about what each side has to do to keep him. Those who want a soft Jesus, gentle and harmless and mostly agreeable, have to quietly lose a whole scene. John tells us that "making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables" (John 2:15). All four Gospels tell of Jesus clearing the temple. The soft Jesus can't survive it. But those who want the warrior Jesus, the man who never showed weakness and never bent, have an even bigger problem, because that Jesus wept. He stood at the grave of his friend Lazarus in front of a crowd and cried, and the Gospel records it without embarrassment: "Jesus wept" (John 11:35).

And that same Jesus, on his last night, "rose from supper. He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist" (John 13:4), and washed his disciples' feet one pair at a time, including the feet of the man he knew would betray him. Notice what John says just before: Jesus knew "that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going back to God" (John 13:3). He didn't kneel because he'd forgotten who he was. He knelt because he knew.

So the question this study keeps circling gets its answer here, and the answer isn't a definition. It's a life. Jesus wept in public, and no one who watched thought, there goes a weak man. He knelt and did the lowest job in the house, and it was the strongest thing in the room, because only a man completely secure in who he is can go that low on purpose. And he cleared the temple, and that wasn't a man losing control. It was strength aimed precisely at the right target, and it stopped where it should.

The men who love the whip deserve a fair hearing, because they're making a point a soft church needs to hear. Plenty of men quote the temple scene against a Christianity they find limp and allergic to any strength at all, and they aren't entirely wrong. Jesus wasn't harmless. A manhood with no capacity for anger at evil isn't more Christlike than an angry one. It's less, because it can't be moved by the things that move the heart of God.

But this is where the whip exposes the strongman instead of endorsing him. Look at what Jesus was angry about. "Is it not written, 'My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations'? But you have made it a den of robbers" (Mark 11:17). He was angry that his Father's house had been turned into a marketplace, that the place of prayer meant for every nation had been crowded with trade. He was never angry, with whip or word, at an insult to himself. When they mocked him, he was silent. When they struck him, he didn't strike back. When they nailed him to the cross, he prayed, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34). The same man and the same strength, and it never once fired in his own defense. Our anger is rarely like that. It's usually about us, our honor, our being disrespected, our will crossed, and then we reach for the temple story to make our temper sound holy.

So here's the definition the session has been working toward. Strength isn't the absence of feeling, or Jesus was weak at the grave. And it isn't the presence of force, or Jesus was strong only for the few minutes he held the whip. Strength is power under control, all of it available and all of it aimed, not at the defense of the self, but at the good of others and the glory of God. The clearest picture of it isn't the whip. It's the garden, where Jesus tells Peter to put his sword back and says, "Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels?" (Matthew 26:53). He had all the strength there is, and he held out his hands to be bound. That's the measure of a man. Lay every other version of masculinity against it, the strongman, the passive man and every cartoon in between, and none of them passes.

scriptureStudy.note: "Jesus wept." The Gospel records the strongest man who ever lived crying openly at a friend's grave, without apology or embarrassment. Feeling deeply and showing it cost him none of his strength.

"If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet." Jesus takes a servant's task in front of his own disciples and then tells them to do the same. Greatness is measured downward, and the lowest service becomes a mark of the deepest security.

"And making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple." The scene is real and fierce, and it rules out any harmless Jesus. But the anger is aimed at what had been done to his Father's house, precise and purposeful, never a tantrum and never a defense of his own honor.

"Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city." Scripture ranks the man who governs his own spirit above the conqueror. Self-command is the higher strength, the very quality the strongman lacks.

"Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart." Jesus describes his own heart as gentle and lowly. Gentleness here isn't a concession to weakness but the character of the strongest man, freely chosen.

"Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels?" At his arrest Jesus names the power available to him and then sets it aside. That's strength under control: capacity fully present and fully surrendered to the Father's will.

"A bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench." The prophet's picture of God's servant is overwhelming strength that handles the fragile with great care, power so complete it can be trusted with what is nearly broken.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, look at what strength under control actually is, because it's easy to say and hard to live. The older Christian and classical traditions had a name for it, temperance or self-mastery. They didn't mean only abstaining from pleasure. They meant a man whose desires answer to his reason and whose reason answers to God, so that his whole force is available and none of it runs him. Ask how much of this we've lost. The modern picture of the man who is true to himself is often the man who doesn't rule his passions but expresses them, following his anger and his appetite wherever they lead and calling it freedom, when the older wisdom would have called it slavery.

Set this beside Dane Ortlund's Gentle and Lowly (2020), a book-length reading of Matthew 11:29, a reminder that the deepest thing about the strongest man was tenderness freely given. Then take the hard cultural turn. Our moment produces online strongmen who market a masculinity of dominance, appetite and the refusal ever to be crossed. They draw young men because the hunger for strength is real and God-given. But what they offer is passion off the leash, and a man ruled by his anger and his appetite isn't powerful. He's ruled by the very things he thinks he commands. The measure that exposes every counterfeit is the same: the man who could have called for legions of angels and let himself be led to the cross, every capacity intact and every capacity answering to his Father. Strength under control is neither the suppression of feeling nor its indulgence, but its government, under God, for the good of others.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group is admired for being unflappable. He never loses his temper, never raises his voice, never lets anyone see him rattled, and he takes real pride in it. When the session names strength as power under control, he assumes it's describing him.

His self-command may be exactly what the session commends, and if so, say so. But there are two kinds of control. There's the control of a man whose strength answers to God and is fully available when real wrong calls for it. And there's the control of a man who has simply gone numb, who never gets angry because he never lets himself feel much of anything, whose calm isn't mastery but absence. The first can weep at a grave and clear a temple. The second can do neither, and may mistake his flatness for peace.

Don't assume you know which he is. Honor the discipline if it's real, and still ask, gently, whether his composure has ever broken for the right reason, whether he can be moved by a wrong done to someone else, or whether the same wall that keeps his anger in also keeps his heart out.

memoryVerse.text: Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city.

sessions.title: Emotional Honesty, Friendship, and the Silence That Kills
sessions.aim: To face the trained silence that isolates men and, at its far edge, kills them, and to recover truthfulness about what a man carries and real friendship as strengths rather than weaknesses, refusing both the stoic picture that calls silence composure and the sentimental one that mistakes venting for depth, and keeping a clear path to real help in view for any man in real danger.
sessions.summary:
Ask a man how many people he can be completely truthful with, and he may land on one. Some will land on none. We were trained young that a man handles it himself and that needing someone is weakness, so many men have built lives full of contacts and empty of friends: surrounded, and unknown. Men who will do almost anything for each other won't do the one thing that would help most, which is to say out loud that they're not okay.

Scripture doesn't call that strength. "Two are better than one," the Preacher says, "But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!" (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10). There's a real case for stoic composure: a man shouldn't unload every feeling on everyone, and restraint can be a service to the people who depend on him. That's true, and venting isn't the same as truthfulness. But the stoic ideal has a body count. Men die by suicide at several times the rate of women, and the trained silence is part of that story.

The silence a man calls strength is often the thing most likely to destroy him, and underneath the refusal to be known is fear: if they saw the real me, they'd leave. Jesus had friends, wept in front of them, told them "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Mark 14:34), and asked them to stay near. If the strongest man who ever lived wouldn't carry it alone, the strength your silence seems to prove isn't strength.

keyScripture.why: "Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow" (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10). The Preacher goes on to pity the man "who is alone when he falls." Being alone is named as the danger, and the presence of another is the difference between falling and being lifted.

discussion.q: Who is the one person you can be completely truthful with about how you're doing? If the answer is no one, when did you decide you didn't need one?
discussion.behind: Open this gently and without shaming the man whose answer is zero. Many men will realize in the silence that they can't name a single friend who really knows them. Don't rush to fix it. Let the answer land, and treat a man's truthfulness about his isolation as the first crack of light, not a failure to correct.

discussion.q: Where did you learn that a man handles it himself and that needing someone is weakness? What has carrying everything alone actually cost you?
discussion.behind: Trace the lesson to its source and its price. It usually came from a father, a coach, a culture, taught early and enforced hard. Help men connect the rule they absorbed to the isolation they live in now: the marriage a wife can't get inside, the friendships that stay on the surface. Often the cost is a loneliness they've stopped noticing. Go first.

discussion.q: Some men believe they shouldn't burden others and that composure is a service to the people who depend on them. What's true in that, and where does composure turn into a silence that's slowly isolating you?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves with care, because this is where a man can hide. Restraint is real, and venting on everyone isn't the goal. But the stoic ideal can become a prison, and the man who never lets anyone in isn't serving his family; he's going hungry in front of them. Help the room find the line between mature restraint and a deadly silence, without shaming the private man into more hiding.

discussion.q: Read Mark 14:32-42. Jesus tells Peter, James and John, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Remain here and watch" (Mark 14:34). What does it do to your idea of strength that the strongest man who ever lived wouldn't go through that night alone?
discussion.behind: Men will agree in theory that isolation is bad and still believe deep down that their own silence is strength. Gethsemane breaks that, because Jesus did the opposite: he named his anguish and asked his friends to stay. Let the room sit with the fact that going it alone in suffering isn't more Christlike than Jesus. It's less.

discussion.q: Underneath the refusal to be known, there's often a fear that if people saw the real you, they'd leave. Is that fear in you? Is there a true thing you've never said out loud to another man?
discussion.behind: This is the center of the session, and for some man in the room it isn't theoretical, so handle it with real care. Keep the path to help in view: some weights need a counselor, a pastor or a crisis line, not just a friend. Invite truthfulness without forcing anyone to disclose anything, and make it clear the room and the leader are safe. Never leave a man who opens up standing alone in it.

objections.objection: A man should not go around dumping his feelings on everyone. Keeping it together is exactly how I protect my family and do my job, and all this pressure to open up just turns men into a mess of emotions who cannot function.
objections.response: This draws a real distinction, and the study means to keep it. There's a difference between being truthful with a few trusted people and unloading every passing feeling on everyone in range. The second isn't a virtue. It's exhausting, and venting isn't depth. So the instinct to protect others from your every mood isn't wrong. But watch what "keeping it together" can hide. It can name a healthy restraint, and it can name a slow death, and only you know which one you're living. Protecting your family doesn't require being unknown to them. A man who keeps it together so completely that his wife and children never see his heart isn't sheltering them. He's living behind a wall in the same house. The goal isn't to make you a mess. It's to let a few safe people past the wall, so that the strength you're spending to hold everything alone isn't what finally breaks you.

objections.objection: This is just repackaging therapy culture for church men. The last thing the world needs is more men sitting around talking about their feelings instead of taking action and providing for the people who depend on them.
objections.response: The suspicion of therapy culture points at something real. There's a version of it that makes feelings the final authority, treats every discomfort as trauma and mistakes endless talk about yourself for growth, and the study rejects that too. Truthfulness isn't the same as putting feelings on the throne. But don't let the suspicion sell you the idea that action and truthfulness are opposites. Jesus acted more decisively than any man in history, and he also wept in front of his friends and named his anguish out loud in the garden, with no sense that the two contradicted each other. So the real question isn't therapy versus action. It's whether your silence is strength or fear. Men die by suicide at several times the rate of women, many of them having told no one what they carried, and that alone should make an honest man ask whether the stoic ideal he inherited is protecting his people or slowly costing him his life in front of them.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What's the true thing about how you're actually doing that you haven't said out loud to anyone? Who could you say it to this week, if you were willing to be that known?
sessions.practice: This week, tell one true thing to one safe person. Not everything, and not to everyone. Just one plain sentence about how you're actually doing, said out loud to a man you could trust with it, or to your wife, or to a pastor. If you can't think of anyone, that's what you've found, and the practice is to tell God so and ask him for one friend. And if what's true for you is heavier than a friend can carry, tell someone who can help, a pastor, a counselor, a crisis line. Write down what happened in you when you said the true thing instead of carrying it alone.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we were trained to carry it alone and to call the carrying strength, and the weight has been crushing some of us in silence while we smiled and said we were fine. We have contacts and no friends, a house full of people and no one who knows us, and we've believed that if they saw the real thing they would leave. Your Son told his friends his soul was sorrowful even to death and asked them to stay near, and he wasn't weak. Break the silence in us that is slowly killing us. Give us one safe person and the courage to say one true thing, and where the weight is more than a man can bear, send help with a face and a name. Don't let us die alone behind a wall we called strength. Amen.
reflection: Who, if anyone, truly knows how I'm doing, and what does my answer show me about the walls I've built and called strength?
Where did I learn that a man carries it alone, and what has that lesson cost me in marriage, in friendship and in my own soul?
What is the fear underneath my silence? Is it, at bottom, that if someone saw the real me they would leave?
sessions.teaching:
If you ask a man how many people he can be completely himself with, no performance and no editing, many men will land, after a pause, on one. And a troubling number, if they're telling the truth, will land on zero. Not zero friends. They have coworkers and buddies, guys they golf with and text about the game. Zero people who actually know them. In a 2021 national survey by the Survey Center on American Life, 15 percent of American men said they had no close friends at all, up from 3 percent in 1990. Many men have built lives that are crowded and unwitnessed, surrounded and unknown, and they didn't do it by accident. They were trained to. We were taught young that a man handles it himself, that needing someone is a weakness you grow out of, that the strong thing is to carry the weight alone. We learned it so well that we now mistake the isolation it produced for a virtue.

So here's a strange question. Why is it that men, who'll drop everything to help a friend move or fix a car or sit in a hospital waiting room, won't do the one thing that would help themselves, which is to say out loud to another man, "I'm not okay"?

Scripture isn't confused about this, and it doesn't flatter the silence. "Two are better than one," the Preacher says, "because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!" (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10). Being alone isn't described as strength. It's described as peril. The man who has no one is the man in danger.

The case for stoic composure deserves a fair hearing, because there's an honorable version of it and no man should be shamed for having it. It says a man doesn't go around burdening others with his troubles, that keeping it together is a service to the people who depend on him, and that restraint is a mark of maturity. Much of that is true. The man who unloads every feeling on everyone in range is exhausting and a little tyrannical, venting isn't the same as truthfulness, and a father who falls apart on his children is handing them a weight they're too small to carry. Restraint is real.

But there's something the stoic ideal won't look at, and I want us to look at it. It has a body count. Men in this country die by suicide at several times the rate of women, and many die having told no one what they were carrying. I'm not going to let us pretend that the silence we were trained into, and the isolation we call strength, have nothing to do with those numbers.

The silence a man calls his strength is very often the thing most likely to destroy him. And when you get underneath the refusal to be known, it isn't courage at all. It's fear, the kind that has been running the whole performance from the start: if anyone saw the real thing, the failures, the struggle, the parts I've never said out loud, they'd leave. So a man keeps the wall up and calls the wall strength, and stays safe and unknown and slowly starving behind it. A boy who grows up without a father often learns self-reliance early and for good, and wears his ability to carry everything alone like a badge, when it's really just a very tall wall.

Look at the man this study keeps coming back to, because he settles it. Jesus had friends, an inner circle he loved and was known by. He wept in front of them. And in Gethsemane, the night before the cross, he "took with him Peter and James and John, and began to be greatly distressed and troubled. And he said to them, 'My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Remain here and watch'" (Mark 14:33-34). He didn't withdraw into a manly silence and handle it alone. He told his closest friends what was happening in him and asked them to stay near.

The strongest man who ever lived, facing the worst night there has ever been, wouldn't go through it alone. So if you're still telling yourself that your silence is strength and that carrying it alone is what a man does, see what you're claiming: a strength Jesus didn't have and didn't want. The silence isn't the strength. It's a lie, and it's costing men their lives because they're too afraid to say one true word.

scriptureStudy.note: "Two are better than one... For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow." The Preacher goes on to pity the man "who is alone when he falls." Being alone is named as the danger, not the strength, which turns the stoic ideal on its head.
"A threefold cord is not quickly broken." The picture of strength here isn't the solitary man but the braided cord, several strands bound together. Isolation is fragile. Connection lasts.

Jesus "began to be greatly distressed and troubled. And he said to them, 'My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Remain here and watch.'" He names his anguish plainly to his friends and asks them to stay near. No one can call that weakness in the strongest man who ever lived.

"Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another." Real friendship between men isn't soft. It's abrasive and forming, two hard things making each other sharper, and that takes enough closeness to actually make contact rather than the safe distance most men keep.

"Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ." The command assumes burdens too heavy to carry alone and a community meant to carry them together. The man who insists on bearing all his own weight isn't keeping a higher standard. He's refusing this one.

"Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed." Healing is tied to being truthful with another person, so the silence that keeps a man from confession also keeps him from the healing it opens. The wall costs more than loneliness.

"The soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." Scripture records a deep, loyal friendship between two strong men without embarrassment. Closeness between men isn't a threat to their manhood but part of its fullness.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, take up the research on male loneliness and test it against Scripture, because the numbers describe something the older categories barely named. In its 2021 national survey, the Survey Center on American Life found that 15 percent of American men said they had no close friends, five times the share in 1990, and its researchers spoke of a "friendship recession." Grant the finding its weight. It confirms what this session claims: men are more isolated than they'll admit, and it's getting worse. Set beside it the sober, well-established fact that men die by suicide at markedly higher rates than women, a pattern any serious treatment of male silence has to reckon with.

Sebastian Junger, in Tribe (2016), argued that people, soldiers above all, often feel most alive and least alone in shared hardship and purpose, and that modern life strips exactly that away. He's onto something about why men bond in foxholes and struggle in subdivisions. But notice what the research can and can't do. It can measure the isolation and its cost. It can't give a man the courage to be known, which is a spiritual matter, rooted in whether he believes he'd still be loved if he were fully seen. That's where the gospel speaks, because a man who knows he is fully known by God and loved anyway in Christ has ground solid enough to risk being known by another person. A group should sit with the pastoral urgency here, since in almost any room of men there is one nearer the edge than anyone knows, and the aim is both to recover friendship and honesty as strengths and to keep a real path to help, a pastor, a counselor, a crisis line such as the 988 lifeline, plainly visible, so that no man leaves the study believing his silence is a virtue he must keep.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group is the steady one everyone leans on, the friend who's there for everybody, the guy people call in a crisis. He speaks warmly about male friendship and clearly has many friends. When the session asks who really knows him, he goes quiet, and then says, almost lightly, that he's the one others lean on, not the other way around.

Honor his gift before you name the gap. His care for others is real and good. But notice what he just said: no one knows him. He may have made himself the reliable helper precisely so he never has to be the one who needs help. Being the strong one can be its own kind of hiding, a wall built out of service instead of silence. He may be the loneliest man in the room and the least likely to say so.

Don't diminish his care for others. Still ask, gently, when he last let someone carry him, and whether being everyone's strong friend has become the way he keeps from being known. The man who lifts everyone else is exactly the one Scripture warns not to be caught falling alone.

memoryVerse.text: For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!

sessions.title: Servant Leadership Against Domination, and Raising the Next Man
sessions.aim: To read Jesus on greatness the way he meant it, that whoever would be great must be a servant, and to take up the calling every man has to raise or mentor the next man, refusing both the domination that lords authority over others and the abdication that leaves the next generation of men to raise themselves, and grounding it all in the Son of Man who "came not to be served but to serve."
sessions.summary:
On the road to Jerusalem, James and John asked Jesus for the best seats in his glory, and the other ten were furious with them. Every man in the room recognizes that fight. Jesus doesn't settle it by naming a winner. He takes apart the scoreboard: "You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them... But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant... For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:42-45).

The question isn't whether a man will have authority, because every man has some over someone. It's what kind of thing authority is. Domination lords it over people. Servant leadership spends itself for them. There's a fair worry that servant language produces weak leaders who can't make a call, and servanthood isn't spinelessness. But the servant leader isn't the weak man. He's the one strong enough to spend his strength on people who can't pay him back.

This is where the whole study has been heading: the next man. Every man is either raising or mentoring the next generation of men, or leaving them to raise themselves from whatever counterfeit is on sale. And the father wound from session two is either healed and handed on, or passed down intact. A man who lets God father him can father the next man out of what he has received. We become the men we needed, and that's how the wound stops.

keyScripture.why: "You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them... But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant... For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:42-45). Jesus turns greatness upside down and grounds all true authority in his own self-giving.

discussion.q: Read Mark 10:35-45. James and John want the best seats, and the other ten are indignant. Where does the argument about who's greatest still run in you, at work, at home, among other men, and what does winning it get you?
discussion.behind: Start by bringing out the scoreboard every man keeps. The fight over greatness isn't ancient history. It lives in comparison, status and the need to be the most respected man in the room. Notice that the ten were angry too; their anger was the same ambition. Help men name where they still keep score and what the top spot actually buys, which is usually a security that never arrives. Don't settle it yet.

discussion.q: Jesus doesn't name a winner. He says, "But it shall not be so among you" (Mark 10:43). What's your gut reaction to being told the way up is down, and where would that instruction cost you most?
discussion.behind: Men will affirm servant leadership in theory and resist it in the exact place it would cost them. Help each man find the particular place where lording it over people is his habit and serving would be the hard, humbling thing. The point isn't agreement but locating the cost, because that's where the teaching lands.

discussion.q: Some worry that servant language produces weak leaders who can't make a call. What's true in that worry, and where have you seen the difference between a servant leader and a man who is simply passive and calls it humility?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves so servanthood isn't confused with spinelessness. Jesus served and led decisively toward the cross, so servant leadership isn't the absence of decision. Help the room tell the strong man who spends his strength on others from the passive man who abdicates and calls it serving. The study has warned against both since session one.

discussion.q: Read 2 Timothy 2:2. Paul tells Timothy to entrust what he's heard "to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also." Who is the next man in your life, a son, a nephew, a young man at work or church, and what are you actually handing him?
discussion.behind: Turn the room toward the calling the study has been building to. Every man has a next man, whether he's noticed or not, and the choice isn't whether to influence him but what to hand down. Help men name the specific young man they're placed to shape, and be candid about whether they're investing or absent. Keep it concrete.

discussion.q: Malachi ends with a promise that God "will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers" (Malachi 4:6). Where could you become, for the next man, the man you needed and didn't have, and what would it cost you to do it?
discussion.behind: Close the study by closing the circle back to session two. The healing of the father wound comes full circle in fathering the next man out of what you've received. Let the room feel the weight and the hope of it: a man fathered by God can stop a wound that has run for generations by becoming what he lacked. End on the gospel and the calling, not on a to-do list, with each man thinking of the next man's face.

objections.objection: Servant leadership is a nice phrase, but somebody has to actually lead, make hard calls, and take responsibility. If every leader is busy serving and washing feet, you get a directionless mess where nobody is in charge and nothing gets decided.
objections.response: The worry is fair. Leadership does require decision, direction and a willingness to carry responsibility, and a servanthood in which no one ever leads isn't what Jesus showed us. But the objection assumes that serving and leading are opposites, and the man who taught servant leadership led more decisively than anyone in history.
