Mark says that on the road to Jerusalem "Jesus was walking ahead of them" (Mark 10:32), toward a cross no one else would carry, and he made every hard call his mission required. Servant leadership isn't the absence of leading. It's leading aimed differently: authority spent on the good of the people led rather than the glory of the leader. The servant leader still decides, still carries the weight and still goes first, but he does it for his people and not for his standing, and he walks into the cost himself rather than sending others. That isn't a directionless mess. It's the only leadership strong enough to be trusted, because the people under it can see it's being spent for them, not used on them.

objections.objection: I never had a father worth mentioning, so who am I to mentor anyone? I do not have it together enough to be handing wisdom to some younger guy. That is for men who actually had it figured out, which I did not.
objections.response: That's a real and common fear, but the conclusion runs backward. The man who was never fathered isn't disqualified from fathering the next man. He may be especially fit for it, because he knows exactly what was missing and exactly what the next man is starving for, having gone without it himself. You don't mentor out of having everything figured out. No one has that. You mentor out of what God has done and is doing in you, out of the wound he's healing, not the one you're hiding. The men who had it handed to them easily are sometimes the worst at handing it down, because they never had to think about it. Let God father you first, and then father the next man out of what you've received. We become the men we needed. The boy you were, with the empty chair, is exactly why some younger man needs you to step in now, not perfect, just present, which is the thing you didn't get and can now give.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Who is the next man watching you right now? If he became the man you're actually modeling, rather than the one you talk about, would you be glad?
sessions.practice: This week, take one concrete step toward the next man. If you have a son, do the thing with him you keep meaning to do, and while you do it, tell him one true thing about being a man. If you don't, find the young man already near you, the nephew, the new guy at work, the kid at church with no father around, and start one real conversation. Not a lecture, just presence and attention. And privately, ask God to father you enough that you have something to hand down. Write down what it stirred in you to be, for a moment, the man you needed and didn't have.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, you ended the argument about who is greatest by taking up a towel and a cross, and you told us plainly it shall not be so among us, that the way up is down, that the great are servants and the first are slaves of all. Forgive the scoreboards we keep, the authority we spend on ourselves, the times we've lorded it over the people we were called to serve. You came not to be served but to serve, and to give your life as a ransom, and we have wanted to be served and called it leadership. Make us servants strong enough to spend our strength on people who can't pay us back. And for the next man watching us, the son, the young man with no father near, let us become by your grace the men we needed and never had, so that the wound stops here and what is good is handed on. Amen.
reflection: Where do I still keep a scoreboard of my own greatness, and what am I trying to secure by being the most respected man in the room?
Is my authority, wherever I have it, being spent on the good of the people under it, or on my own standing and comfort?
Who is the next man watching me, and am I handing him the wound I received or the healing I've found, presence or absence, a hand on his shoulder or a chair left empty?
sessions.teaching:
On the road up to Jerusalem, James and John came to Jesus and asked for the seats at his right and left hand in his glory. When the other ten heard about it, Mark says, "they began to be indignant at James and John" (Mark 10:41). Even at the Last Supper, Luke tells us, "a dispute also arose among them, as to which of them was to be regarded as the greatest" (Luke 22:24). Nobody has to explain that fight to a room of men. It's the same jockeying for the top spot, the comparing and the need to be the most respected man in the room, that men have always known.

Notice what Jesus doesn't do with it. He doesn't settle the argument by naming a winner, and he doesn't coach them to compete better. He takes apart the scoreboard they're fighting over. "You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them" (Mark 10:42). That's the world's picture of greatness, the man on top with everyone beneath him, and every one of the twelve understood it because every one of them wanted it. Then Jesus says, "But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all" (Mark 10:43-44). Not a better version of the ranking. Not the same pyramid with nicer men at the top. Something different. And he grounds it not in a rule but in himself: "For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45).

So the question isn't whether a man will have authority. Every man already has some, over children, a team, a household, a younger man who watches him. The question is what kind of thing that authority is, and Jesus says it's the reverse of what the world taught us. Domination lords it over the people beneath you. Servant leadership spends itself for the people entrusted to you. One uses the led for the leader. The other uses the leader for the led.

The case for strong, decisive leadership deserves a fair hearing, because thoughtful men make it and it's guarding something real. The worry is that all this servant language produces weak leaders, men who can't make a hard call or carry the weight of a decision, who hide their passivity behind the word humility and leave everyone waiting for direction that never comes. That worry is legitimate. Servanthood isn't spinelessness, and this study has been against the passive man since the first session. But the worry misreads the servant. Look at the one who taught it. Mark says that on that same road "Jesus was walking ahead of them" (Mark 10:32). He led more decisively than any man who ever lived, made every hard call his mission required, and went straight toward a cross no one else would carry, and he did all of it as a servant. The servant leader isn't the man too weak to lead. He's the man strong enough to spend his strength on people who can never pay him back.

That brings us to the calling every session has been quietly heading toward: the next man. No man gets to opt out of this. Every man is either raising or mentoring the next generation of men, or leaving them to raise themselves on whatever counterfeit is selling that year, the influencer, the algorithm, the strongman, the void. There's no neutral option, no way to stand aside and hand down nothing, because absence is handed down too. The empty chair teaches. Your sons are learning manhood from you whether you're teaching on purpose or not. The young men around you, the nephew, the new hire, the kid at church whose father is gone, are watching some man to learn what a man is, and if it isn't you it will be someone, and someone worse is always available. Paul saw the chain plainly: "what you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also" (2 Timothy 2:2).

And this closes the circle back to the father wound. That wound is either healed and handed on, or passed down intact. A man who wasn't fathered will do one of two things with it. He'll let God father him, receive as a gift the approval he was starving for, and then father the next man out of what he finally received. Or he'll hand the wound down whole, the same absence, the same coldness, the same silence, to a boy who will spend his own life carrying it. The last book of the Old Testament ends with the promise that God "will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers" (Malachi 4:6). That turning is what God is after.

This is where I'm most fully inside this study, because it's my own life. I was raised without a father, and I have five sons, and the whole point is that the wound stops here, that they get the presence I didn't, that they learn what a man is from a man who is there on purpose and not from a vacancy. We become the men we needed. That's servant leadership at its root: a man spending himself to give the next man what he never got. It's the towel and the basin, carried into the next generation. And it's how the wound finally stops.

scriptureStudy.note: "You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them... But it shall not be so among you." Jesus names the world's model of authority, domination from above, and forbids it among his people. He doesn't offer a gentler version of the same climb. He turns it over.

"Whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve." Greatness is redefined as service and grounded in Jesus himself, who had all authority and spent it on people who couldn't repay him.

"For I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you." After washing feet, Jesus makes the act a pattern to copy. Servant leadership isn't a mood but a practice, set out so it would be handed on.

"What you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also." Paul names four links in one sentence, himself, Timothy, faithful men and others, making the handing-down of the faith a command, not an extra.

"And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise." The handing-down happens in ordinary life, which means fathering the next man is less a program than a presence, the daily nearness many fatherless men never had.

"And he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers." The closing book of the Old Testament in Christian Bibles ends with a promise to heal the breach between fathers and children, naming that mending as something God himself comes to do.

"Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant." The mind a man is to have is the mind of one who held the highest place and went down into service, the root of every towel taken up and every next man served.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, look at both halves of this session, servant leadership and the handing-down of manhood, because each has a history. On authority, Jesus isn't softening the world's model. He's overturning a pattern as old as power itself. Ask how often the church has failed here, taking up again and again the very lording-it-over Jesus forbade and dressing domination in religious language. The right response to Mark 10 is repentance, not only admiration. Set this beside a plain observation about our own time: many young men, cut off from fathers and mentors, are being formed instead by online figures who sell exactly the domination Jesus rejected. The appeal is real because the hunger for a man to follow is real and God-given, so the answer isn't to shame the hunger but to put a true man, and the true Man, in front of it.

On the handing-down, look at the pairs Scripture gives us: Moses and Joshua, Elijah and Elisha, Paul and Timothy. Scripture assumes faith and maturity pass from person to person, up close and over time, not absorbed from the air, and that's exactly what the modern breakdown has interrupted. Then take the most hopeful turn in the study. The healing of the father wound isn't complete until it's handed on, because grace received tends toward grace given, and a man truly fathered by God becomes a father to the next man almost as its natural fruit. Sit with the sober fact that the wound is passed down by default and stopped only on purpose, and with the hope that one man, fathered by God, can be the place it stops.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group is a strong leader, successful, respected and decisive, the kind of man others follow. He embraces servant leadership warmly, sure he already practices it, and points to how much he does for his team and his family. But when the session turns to the next man, he goes quiet. His sons are grown now and the relationship is distant, and a younger man at work who once looked up to him has drifted away.

Honor his strength before you name the ache. He's a capable leader, and much of his service is real, so say so. But it's possible to lead a company well and father the next man poorly, to excel at the world's greatness and be absent from the kind Jesus named. His quiet is worth a gentle question, because the distance from his sons may be the place this study is actually aimed at him.

Don't shame him, and don't treat his success as failure. Ask, gently, whether the strength that built his standing was ever spent on the next man the way Jesus spent his, and whether it's too late, which it rarely is, to turn his heart toward a son or a young man while there's still time.

memoryVerse.text: For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

leaderPrimer:
The particular danger of a men's study is that men will turn it into a contest. They'll perform strength for each other, agree loudly with every point that convicts some other kind of man, and keep the wall up the whole time, so that five weeks go by and nothing true is ever said. A room of men agreeing about manhood in the abstract is one of the safest and most useless places on earth. So set the rule the first night and keep it every night after. No man is here to prove he's a man. We're here to tell the truth, and in this room the truthful man, not the impressive one, is the strong one.

Go first yourself, every time. Men will only go as deep as the leader goes, and if you present yourself as the man who has it handled, the room will perform right back at you and the study will die on contact. Say the true thing about your own father, your own passivity or domination, your own silence, and watch the room breathe out. Some of the most important movement in these sessions will happen in silence: a man realizing he has no real friends, a man feeling an empty chair he has denied for decades, a man seeing that his strength has been aimed at himself the whole time. Make room for that silence instead of asking every man to confess across the circle.

Two things are not optional. First, session two on the father wound and session four on the silence that kills will surface real pain, and in almost any group of men there is one who is closer to the edge than anyone knows, so know your resources before you begin, a pastor, a counselor, a crisis line such as the 988 lifeline, and have them ready, and watch the man who jokes hardest and shares least. If a man discloses that he is in real danger, do not leave him alone in it, stay with him and connect him to real help that night.

Second, keep both counterfeits in view the whole way through. A men's study tilts easily toward the strongman, and you mustn't let it, just as you mustn't let it excuse the passive man. Hold up the one man who was neither, who wept and washed feet and cleared the temple, and measure everything by him.

You don't need to have manhood figured out to lead this. Nobody does. Five weeks won't finish a man. They can show a room of men what their strength was always for, and send them home to a wife, a son, a friend, a next man, quieter and more truthful than they came.

faq.q: Is this study going to tell me to man up and be an alpha, or that masculinity is toxic and I should apologize for it?
faq.a: Neither. Those are the two cartoons the study exists to clear away. Session one names them, the domineering strongman who mistakes volume and control for strength and the passive nice guy who mistakes absence for peace, and then goes back to where Scripture actually starts: a man placed in a garden "to work it and keep it" (Genesis 2:15), given responsibility before any culture handed him a script. The measure the whole study holds up is Jesus, who wept openly, knelt to wash feet, and drove the money changers out of the temple. You won't be told to dominate, and you won't be told your manhood is a problem to be managed. You'll be shown what your strength was for.

faq.q: I was raised without a father, or with a bad one. Is this study going to be painful, and is it safe?
faq.a: It may touch something real, and it's meant to be safe while it does. Session two on the father wound doesn't pry or shame or ask any man to perform his pain. It names that many men carry a wound in one of three forms, the father who left, the father who was there but cold, and the father who was there and cruel, and it brings that wound to the God who calls himself "Father of the fatherless" (Psalm 68:5). Leaders are asked to know their resources before they begin and to watch for the man who is hurting, and no one is ever made to share. If the wound is fresh or heavy, the study points toward real help, a pastor, a counselor, a trusted friend, and treats a man's truthfulness as strength.

faq.q: What if a man in the group is struggling badly, or worse, thinking about ending his life?
faq.a: Take it with complete seriousness. Session four says plainly that men die by suicide at several times the rate of women, and that the trained silence men call strength is part of why. In almost any group of men there is one closer to the edge than anyone knows, and the study is built to make it safe to say so. Leaders are urged in the primer to know their resources before the first night, a pastor, a counselor, a crisis line such as the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and to have them ready. Watch the man who jokes hardest and shares least. If anyone signals real danger, do not leave him alone in it, stay with him, take it seriously, and connect him to real help that night. The point of the whole session is that no man should carry the weight alone, and that saying the true thing out loud is the strong move.

faq.q: Is this just going to be men sitting around talking about their feelings?
faq.a: No, though it does say that being truthful about what you feel is a strength. The man the study points to wept in front of his friends and told them in the garden, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Mark 14:34), and lost none of his strength doing it. But the study keeps a line between truthfulness and venting, between being known by a few trusted people and unloading every feeling on everyone. It rejects the therapy culture that makes feelings the final authority as firmly as it rejects the stoic silence that is isolating men. It holds up a Jesus with a whip as well as tears, and it drives toward action: friendship, presence, the next man. If anything it asks more of a man than the silent version does, because it asks him to be both strong and known.

faq.q: What does the study actually mean by biblical manhood, if it rejects both the tough-guy and the sensitive-guy versions?
faq.a: It means strength given a purpose outside itself. Manhood here isn't dominance proven against other men, and it isn't the absence of strength dressed up as gentleness. It's the picture Scripture opens with, a man put in a garden to work and keep it, strong the way a roof is strong, for the sake of what it shelters. The fullest picture is Jesus, who had all the strength there is and bent it toward the good of the people in front of him, weeping, serving, confronting what was wrong in his Father's house, and finally laying down his life when, as he said, he could have appealed to his Father for "more than twelve legions of angels" (Matthew 26:53). Power under control, aimed at others rather than at the defense of self: that's the strength that shelters a family, keeps a friendship and hands itself down to the next man.

faq.q: The study talks a lot about Jesus as the model of manhood. Was Jesus really strong, or is this the soft Jesus again?
faq.a: It isn't the soft Jesus, and session three won't let either side edit him. The soft reading has to lose the day he made "a whip of cords" and drove the money changers out of the temple (John 2:15). The tough-guy reading has to lose "Jesus wept" (John 11:35) and the night he knelt to wash his disciples' feet. The study keeps the whole man and takes its definition from him: strength isn't the absence of feeling or the mere presence of force, but power under control, all of it available and all of it aimed at the good of others and the glory of God. The clearest picture is the arrest in the garden, where the strongest man who ever lived told Peter to put away his sword and let himself be led away to the cross.

faq.q: Why does the study spend a whole session on men and friendship? That seems minor next to the bigger topics.
faq.a: Because it isn't minor. For some men it's a matter of life and death. Many men, asked who they could be completely truthful with, can name one person, and some can name no one, because they were trained young that a man handles it himself. Scripture calls that aloneness a danger, not a virtue: "woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up" (Ecclesiastes 4:10). The research points the same way. In a 2021 national survey by the Survey Center on American Life, 15 percent of American men said they had no close friends, up from 3 percent in 1990, and men die by suicide at several times the rate of women. The session treats friendship as something a man needs, points to Jesus, who wouldn't face his worst night without his friends near, and won't let any man leave believing his isolation is something to be proud of.

faq.q: I never had it figured out and my own life is a mess. How can I mentor or father the next man?
faq.a: That isn't a disqualification, and session five turns the question around. You don't father or mentor the next man out of having it together, because no man has that. You do it out of what God is doing in you, out of the wound he's healing rather than the one you're hiding. The man who was never fathered often knows best what the next man is starving for, because he starved for it himself. A man fathered by God can father the next man out of what he has received, so the boy you were, with the empty chair, may be exactly why some younger man needs you to step in now, imperfect and present. We become the men we needed.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I have not sorted out my own manhood or my own father stuff?
faq.a: You're the right man to lead it. The study was built for ordinary men, not experts. Every question carries a note on what's behind it, and every session ends in prayer. The real qualification isn't a solved life, which no one has. It's the willingness to go first, to say the true thing about your own father, your own silence and your own counterfeit of strength, because men will only go as deep as the leader goes. If you walk in as the man who has manhood figured out, the room will perform strength right back at you and nothing will move. Your own unfinished struggle, plainly named, is what lets you stand inside the circle with the other men instead of over them. Read the leader primer, settle your own heart before God, and go first.

faq.q: Why does the study keep turning the questions back on the leader and on me, instead of just teaching the material?
faq.a: Because you can't repent of a counterfeit you're still calling strength, and you can't call other men to grow from a height without the call turning into contempt. A study that only pointed at the bad men who aren't in the room would let everyone off the hook and change no one. The control mistaken for leadership, the silence kept rather than admit fear, the anger that feels more like strength than the truth does: these aren't some other kind of man's problems. They're ours. So the questions keep coming back to the leader first, and then to each man, because that's the only place real change can begin.

faq.q: I am not sure I even believe in God. Is there anything here for a skeptic, or is it only for committed Christians?
faq.a: There's something here for you, and you're welcome in the room. You don't have to share the faith to notice that the two versions of manhood on offer, the domineering strongman and the apologetic passive man, are both failing the men who try to live them, and that a great many men are lonely, fatherless and quietly desperate in ways no one is naming. The study puts a particular man in front of you, Jesus, and asks you to look at him without the cartoon: a man who wept and served and confronted wrong and laid down a strength he could have used to save himself. It asks whether that isn't a truer picture of strength than anything else on offer. You're free to finish unconvinced. The study only asks that you not decide in advance that a manhood measured by that man isn't worth considering.

faq.q: Does taking manhood this seriously mean the study looks down on women, or thinks men are more important?
faq.a: No, and it's careful here. To say that Scripture speaks to men as men, calls them to a particular faithfulness and names particular failures of manhood isn't to say that men matter more or women less, any more than a study written for women would be an insult to men. The study holds the equal dignity of women as bearers of God's image throughout, names the harm domineering men have done to women as sin, and holds up a manhood whose whole aim is to shelter and serve rather than to rule. The point of taking manhood seriously isn't to raise men over anyone. It's to call men to become the kind of men the people around them, women very much included, can rest under rather than brace against.

timeline.event: Genesis 2 places the first man in the garden "to work it and keep it" (Genesis 2:15), giving him labor and responsibility before any culture defines masculinity, so that manhood begins as stewardship and protection rather than conquest.

Genesis 3 records a failure that comes before Cain's violence: the man is "with her" (Genesis 3:6) while the serpent works and says nothing, protects nothing, and eats. The first failure of manhood in Scripture is passivity that looks like presence.

David, called a man after God's own heart and also a man of blood, carries the whole tension of manhood in one life: strength given to God, and strength turned against Uriah and Bathsheba. The same power can shelter or destroy.

Malachi, the closing book of the Old Testament in Christian Bibles, ends with the promise that God "will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers" (Malachi 4:6), naming the breach between fathers and children as something God comes to mend.

Jesus gives the fullest picture of manhood: weeping at a friend's grave, kneeling to wash his disciples' feet, driving the money changers from the temple, and laying down his life when he could have appealed for "more than twelve legions of angels" (Matthew 26:53).

Paul tells the Corinthians to "act like men, be strong" and in the next breath, "Let all that you do be done in love" (1 Corinthians 16:13-14), joining the call to strength and the call to love so that neither the strongman nor the passive man can claim the verse.

Augustine writes the Confessions, telling of a father, Patricius, who was ambitious for his son's career and was baptized only near the end of his life, and of his own disordered desires and restless heart until grace found him: an early and searching account of a man's inner disorder and its healing.

The Industrial Revolution moves much paid work out of the home and sends fathers to the factory and the office, breaking the daily apprenticeship by which many boys had learned manhood at a father's side, an argument Nancy Pearcey develops in her history of the subject.

Robert Bly's Iron John gives voice to a secular men's movement grieving the father wound and the loss of male initiation. It names the ache well, though it reaches for myth rather than the gospel for the answer.

John Eldredge's Wild at Heart persuades many Christian men that they were made for desire, adventure and strength, correcting a domesticated ideal while risking a picture of manhood as fundamentally untamed. The study weighs both sides.

Nancy Pearcey's The Toxic War on Masculinity traces the history of the masculinity debates and argues from sociological research that churchgoing Christian men, far from matching the stereotype, are among the most engaged husbands and fathers, complicating the culture-war picture in both directions.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thanks for being here. It takes something for a man to walk into a room and talk truthfully about being a man. Before we start, three things. First, nobody here is trying to prove he's a man. We're not here to impress each other. In this room the truthful man is the strong one, not the impressive one. Second, none of us has manhood figured out, and what's said here stays here. It never becomes ammunition later. Third, we're not talking about some other kind of man out there tonight. We're talking about ourselves, and I'm in that too. One more thing, and I mean it. Some of what we touch, the empty chair, the silence men carry, will be real and heavy. If anyone here is struggling badly, you're not alone in it, and I'm available, tonight, to talk and to help. Tonight we're looking at this together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we'll sit with it before anyone says a word. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only true ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what the passage says. Now let's bring it home, off the page and into the life each of us walked in from tonight: the marriage, the kids, the friendships, the work, the man in the mirror. None of this matters if it stays an idea about manhood in general.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there, even though it isn't tied up, because a man isn't remade in an evening. Take what we've talked about home rather than leaving it at the door. Try the practice this week, even if you do it badly. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. And come back ready to be truthful, not finished. Let me pray for us before we go. Thank you for being in this room, and hear me: my door is open if any of you needs it.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about honesty over performance and not proving anything, and walk session 1's opening questions slowly.
Week 2: Session 1, What Manhood Is For, Past the Caricatures, full discussion and practice.
Week 3: Session 2, The Father Wound and the God Who Fathers the Fatherless, with extended time and care, and private availability for anyone the session touches.
Week 4: Session 3, Strength Under Control, the Man Jesus Was, part one, reading the tears, the basin, and the whip together.
Week 5: Session 3 continued, working the definition of strength as power under control into each man's actual anger and standing.
Week 6: Session 4, Emotional Honesty, Friendship, and the Silence That Kills, with resources ready and a watchful eye on the room.
Week 7: Session 5, Servant Leadership Against Domination, and Raising the Next Man.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit all five practices, the scripture index, and the next man each guy is now aiming at, closing in the Son of Man who came to serve.

bibliography.title: Gentle and Lowly: The Heart of Christ for Sinners and Sufferers
bibliography.author: Dane C. Ortlund
bibliography.note: A book-length reading of Matthew 11:29, where Jesus calls himself "gentle and lowly in heart" (2020). Background for strength under control in session 3 and the Father's heart in session 2.

bibliography.title: The Toxic War on Masculinity: How Christianity Reconciles the Sexes
bibliography.author: Nancy R. Pearcey
bibliography.note: A history of the masculinity debates (2023) that draws on sociological research about churchgoing men and traces how industrialization pulled fathers out of the home. Background for sessions 1 and 5 and the timeline.

bibliography.title: Wild at Heart: Discovering the Secret of a Man's Soul
bibliography.author: John Eldredge
bibliography.note: An influential case (2001) that men were made for desire, adventure and strength. Session 1 takes it up as the strongest form of the call to recover masculine strength, granting what's true in it and asking where it slides toward caricature.

bibliography.title: The Boy Crisis: Why Our Boys Are Struggling and What We Can Do About It
bibliography.author: Warren Farrell and John Gray
bibliography.note: A gathering of research on father absence and its effects on boys (2018). A secular book that describes the problem carefully. Background for sessions 2 and 5.

bibliography.title: Of Boys and Men: Why the Modern Male Is Struggling
bibliography.author: Richard V. Reeves
bibliography.note: A data-driven account (2022) of the struggles of men and boys in education, work and family life. Background for sessions 1 and 4. It describes the problem well and doesn't claim to offer a spiritual answer.

bibliography.title: Tribe: On Homecoming and Belonging
bibliography.author: Sebastian Junger
bibliography.note: On why people, soldiers especially, bond most deeply in shared hardship and purpose and struggle in modern isolation (2016). Background for the friendship material of session 4.

bibliography.title: Adam's Return: The Five Promises of Male Initiation
bibliography.author: Richard Rohr
bibliography.note: A treatment of male initiation and the father wound from the contemplative tradition (2004). Background for sessions 2 and 5, to be read with discernment and tested against Scripture.

bibliography.title: Why Does He Do That? Inside the Minds of Angry and Controlling Men
bibliography.author: Lundy Bancroft
bibliography.note: A secular resource on the patterns of control and abuse (2002), so leaders can tell the difference between ordinary struggle and real harm when the strongman material comes up in sessions 1 and 5. Pair it with local help.

bibliography.title: Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: The fourth-century account of a man's restless heart, his disordered desires, his parents, and his conversion. Cited in the timeline and useful background for session 2.

bibliography.title: Disciplines of a Godly Man
bibliography.author: R. Kent Hughes
bibliography.note: A practical and widely used book (1991) on the ordinary habits of Christian manhood: prayer, purity, friendship, fathering. A companion for men who want concrete next steps after sessions 4 and 5.

bibliography.title: The Gospel of Mark
bibliography.author: the evangelist Mark
bibliography.note: The book behind session 5, where Jesus answers the argument about greatness with the Son of Man who "came not to be served but to serve" (Mark 10:45). Read it, don't only cite it.

bibliography.title: The Gospel of John
bibliography.author: the evangelist John
bibliography.note: The book behind session 3, where Jesus weeps at the grave, washes his disciples' feet and clears the temple. Read it straight through alongside the study.

furtherReading: Gentle and Lowly, Dane Ortlund, for men who want to sit longer with the heart of Christ behind sessions 2 and 3.
The Toxic War on Masculinity, Nancy Pearcey, for those who want the history behind the caricatures of session 1 and the research that complicates the culture-war picture.
Of Boys and Men, Richard Reeves, for readers who want the research on the struggles of men and boys today.
Why Does He Do That, Lundy Bancroft, for anyone who needs to understand the patterns of control and abuse that the study refuses to call strength.
The Gospel of John, read straight through, for men willing to watch the strongest man who ever lived weep, wash feet and clear a temple, and to let that man be the measure.

glossary.definition: As this study uses the phrase: not dominance proven against other men, and not the absence of strength dressed as gentleness, but strength given a purpose outside itself, strong the way a roof is strong, for the sake of what it shelters. Measured by Jesus, who bent all his strength toward the good of others.

The caricature of manhood as dominance, volume and the refusal ever to be crossed. Its strength is aimed at defending the self, and underneath it runs the fear of looking weak. One of the two counterfeits the study refuses.

The caricature of manhood as absence: the man who calls his silence peace and his avoidance humility. Its first form is Adam standing beside his wife in the garden and saying nothing. The other counterfeit, and the first failure of manhood in Scripture.

The lasting mark left by a father who was absent, or present and cold, or present and cruel. It can hide for decades and surface as a hunger for approval, a surprising anger, or a certainty that one is alone. It's healed not by finally getting from the father what he never gave, but by being fathered by God.
The name God gives himself in Psalm 68:5. Not a distant deity, but a Father who takes up the place a missing or failing father left empty.

The study's definition of strength: neither the absence of feeling nor the presence of force, but power held under command, all of it available and all of it aimed at the good of others rather than the defense of self. Its picture is Jesus at his arrest, with every power at hand, letting himself be led to the cross.

Anger at real wrong done to others and to God's name, precise and purposeful, as when Jesus cleared the temple. It's different from the strongman's anger, which almost always defends an insult to himself.

The trained male silence that isolates a man and mistakes refusing to be known for strength. At its far edge it is part of why men die by suicide at far higher rates. Its cure is truthfulness and real friendship, which Scripture treats as strength.

Authority spent on the good of the people it serves rather than the glory of the one who holds it, as Jesus taught in Mark 10:42-45. Not the absence of decision but its redirection, strength strong enough to be spent on people who can't repay it.

The world's model of authority that Jesus forbade among his people: "those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them" (Mark 10:42). It uses the led for the leader, and the strongman, online and off, keeps selling it to fatherless young men.

The son, nephew, younger coworker or fatherless boy whom every man is either raising and mentoring or leaving to raise himself from whatever counterfeit is on sale. There's no neutral option, because absence is handed down too.

The closing idea of the study: a man fathered by God can father the next man out of what he has received, giving the younger one the presence, blessing and instruction he himself lacked, so that the father wound stops instead of being passed down.

Charles Taylor's term (A Secular Age, 2007) for the modern self, sealed off and self-defining. Applied here to the man with no father to receive manhood from and no purpose outside himself, who has to make his own meaning by performance, and so either keeps proving or keeps hiding.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Most men were handed two versions of manhood and told to pick: the swaggering one that mistakes volume for strength and the soft one that mistakes absence for peace. Most of us suspect the truth is neither. This five-session study clears away the caricatures and asks what manhood is actually for. It looks at the father wound and the God who fathers the fatherless, at strength under control in the man who wept, washed feet and drove out the money changers, at the silence that is isolating men, and at servant leadership set against domination, ending with the calling every man has to raise or mentor the next one. Any man can lead it. Come truthful, not finished.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We're starting a five-week study for men, and before anyone braces for a lecture on manning up, it isn't that, and it isn't the opposite either. It clears away the two caricatures our culture keeps selling, the domineering tough guy and the passive nice guy, and holds up one man as the measure: Jesus, who wept, washed feet and drove out the money changers, strength completely under control. It speaks plainly about the father wound, names the silence that is hurting men, and calls every man to raise the next one. No homework, and you don't need to be an expert to lead a group. Sign up at the welcome table.

quoteCards: The first failure of the first man wasn't violence. It was silence. Adam was right there, and said nothing.
Manhood isn't dominance proven against other men. It's strength given a purpose outside itself.
Most men never got from their father what they needed. The healing is being fathered by God now.
"Father of the fatherless" doesn't mean God helps you find closure. It means God takes the empty chair.
Jesus wept, and no one thought him weak. He washed feet, and it was the strongest thing in the room.
Strength isn't the absence of feeling or the presence of force. It's power under control.
The silence a man calls his strength is very often the thing most likely to destroy him.
Every man is raising the next man, or leaving him to raise himself. There's no neutral option.
We become the men we needed. That's how the wound stops.
